title: I built a playable transport tycoon game in one week with Claude and Codex
author: ventayol
selftext:
I use AI for almost everything at work. This summer I started building side projects in my spare time to see where its limits were when I used it through every stage, from the first idea to getting something into people’s hands.



https://reddit.com/link/1xwz6c9/video/bckmd3svus1i1/player

One of those projects, [Bolets](https://bolets.app/), has become a go-to reference for mushroom foragers in Catalonia, with maps and local guides that help people decide where and when to head out. After building Bolets and Finsails, I wanted to see how far I could get with a game. I started Fourways from scratch and had a playable preview one week later, working on it in my spare time alongside my regular full-time job.



Fourways is an isometric transport tycoon game inspired by OpenTTD. In the clip, I connect a coal mine to a power station, lay track and build platforms, then buy a steam locomotive and send it out for its first delivery. From there you might add a passing loop to run a second train, connect two towns by bus, or build a port where trucks and trains feed the same ships.



The map changes as you play. Towns grow, industries change what they produce and need, and rival companies build their own routes. You start in the steam era and can work your way up to electric freight and high-speed rail. A line that paid for your expansion in the 1950s might need a different job a few decades later.



I used Claude and Codex throughout the project. In Godot, the game generates its art, music, and sound in code. One of the playtests drives the interface through building that first coal route and checks that the delivery actually earns money. That gave me a way to check that track construction, vehicle orders, cargo, and the economy still worked together as the game changed.



The preview is free for Windows and Mac. I’m happy to answer any questions about how I built it. If you’ve built a simulation with AI, I’d also love to hear how you tested that the different systems still worked together as the project grew.
